source_refs.quote: sub-let, assigned or otherwise parted with the possession
These three expressions deal with different concepts and apply to different circumstances.

In subletting there exists the relationship of landlord and tenant as between the tenant and his sub-tenant and all the incidents of letting or tenancy have to be found, namely the transfer of an interest in the estate payment of rent, and the right to possession as against the tenant in respect of the Premises sublet.
In assignment the tenant has to divest himself of all the rights that he has as a tenant.
there must be vesting of possession by the tenant in another person by divesting himself not only of physical possession but also of the right to possession
The divestment or abandonment of the right to possession is necessary in order to invoke the clause of parting with possession
If there is anything in the nature of a right to concurrent user there is no parting with possession
The mere user by other persons is no parting with Possession so long as the tenant retains the legal possession himself

nodes.text: Subject premises: third floor of property bearing No.4-E/7, Jhandewalan Extension, New Delhi

source_refs.quote: the premises described as third floor of property bearing No.4-E/7, Jhandewalan Extension, New Delhi (subject premises)

nodes.text: M/s. Current Advertising and Marketing

source_refs.quote: M/s. Current Advertising and Marketing

nodes.text: M/s. Current Advertising (P) Limited, the first respondent

source_refs.quote: M/s. Current Advertising (P) Limited (the first respondent)

nodes.text: M.L. Aggarwal

source_refs.quote: M.L. Aggarwal

nodes.text: R.P. Aggarwal

source_refs.quote: R.P. Aggarwal

nodes.text: M/s. Censor Advertising Pvt. Ltd., the second respondent

source_refs.quote: M/s. Censor Advertising Pvt. Ltd., (second respondent)

nodes.text: The subject premises were initially let under a lease deed dated 27.06.1979 in the name of M/s. Current Advertising and Marketing

source_refs.quote: the premises described as third floor of property bearing No.4-E/7, Jhandewalan Extension, New Delhi (subject premises), let out initially by a lease deed (Ex.PW-1/R1) dated 27. 06.1979 in the name of a partnership firm described as M/s. Current Advertising and Marketing

nodes.text: M.L. Aggarwal and R.P. Aggarwal were partners in M/s. Current Advertising and Marketing

source_refs.quote: a partnership firm described as M/s. Current Advertising and Marketing in which M.L. Aggarwal and R.P. Aggarwal were partners.

nodes.text: The partnership firm was converted into the private limited company M/s. Current Advertising (P) Limited, the first respondent

source_refs.quote: It is further an admitted fact that the said partnership firm was converted into a private limited company in the name and style of M/s. Current Advertising (P) Limited (the first respondent)

nodes.text: The tenancy rights were transferred to the first respondent, which was accepted as tenant of the subject premises with effect from 27.03.1990

source_refs.quote: It is further undisputed that the tenancy rights were transferred in the name of the first respondent, it having been accepted as the tenancy qua the subject premises with effect from 27.03.1990.

nodes.text: M.L. Aggarwal and R.P. Aggarwal parted ways with effect from April 1992, after which M.L. Aggarwal took over the first respondent company and shifted elsewhere

source_refs.quote: It is admitted that the said Directors of the first respondent company parted ways w.e.f April, 1992 where after one of them, viz., M.L. Aggarwal took over the said company, having shifted elsewhere

nodes.text: R.P. Aggarwal continued on the subject premises retaining control

source_refs.quote: the other Director (R.P. Aggarwal) continuing on the subject premises retaining its control.

nodes.text: The subject premises came to be in the use and occupation of the second respondent, M/s. Censor Advertising Pvt. Ltd.

source_refs.quote: The subject premises concededly came to be in use and occupation of M/s. Censor Advertising Pvt. Ltd., (second respondent)

nodes.text: It was alleged that the first respondent tenant sub-let the subject premises to the second respondent without the landlord's previous written consent

source_refs.quote: the first respondent (the tenant) had sub- let the subject premises to the second respondent without the previous consent in writing of the landlord

nodes.text: The trial court found that the petitioners had failed to prove the ground of subletting and dismissed the petition on that ground

source_refs.quote: The trial court, however, was of the view that the petitioners had failed to prove the CM(M) 433/2013 Page 2 of 5 ground of subletting and, thus, dismissed the petition on that ground.

nodes.text: The referenced prior matter was dismissed by judgment dated 15.12.2012

source_refs.quote: the said having been dismissed by the judgment dated 15.12.2012.

source_refs.quote: let out initially by a lease deed (Ex.PW-1/R1) dated 27. 06.1979 in the name of a partnership firm described as M/s. Current Advertising and Marketing

source_refs.quote: a company in which R.P. Aggarwal is a Director.

source_refs.quote: If there is anything in the nature of a right to concurrent user there is no parting with possession
The mere user by other persons is no parting with Possession so long as the tenant retains the legal possession himself
A tenant cannot be said to part with the possession of any part of the premises unless his agreement with the license wholly ousts him from the legal possession of that part.

LAW:S02:DRC14:1b.text:
Notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in any other law or contract, no order or decree for the recovery of possession of any premises shall be made by any court or Controller in favour of the landlord against a tenant:Provided that the Controller may, on an application made to him in the prescribed manner, make an order for the recovery of possession of the premises on one or more of the following grounds only, namely: -
cite11†(b) that the tenant has, on or after the 9th day of June, 1952, sub-let, assigned or otherwise parted with the possession of the whole or any part of the premises without obtaining the consent in writing of the landlord;

IK-190902:L107.text: 30. So long as the lessee retains the legal possession of the whole of the premises he does not commit a breach of law against parting with the possession by allowing other people to use the same. A tenant cannot be said to part with the possession of any part of the premises unless his agreement with the license wholly ousts him from the legal possession of that part. If there is anything in the nature of a right to concurrent user there is no parting with possession: See Stenina v.

IK-190902:L108.text: Abrahama, (1931) f Ch D 470 and G. D. Chaudhary v. Anand Sarup. 1966 Delhi Lt 28.

IK-190902:L109.text: 31. Clause (b) of the proviso to cite8†Section 14(1) uses three expressions namely 'sublet', 'assign' and 'otherwise parted with the possession of the whole or any part of the premises without obtaining the consent in writing of the landlord'. These three expressions deal with different concepts and apply to different circumstances.

IK-190902:L110.text: In subletting there exists the relationship of landlord and tenant as between the tenant and his sub-tenant and all the incidents of letting or tenancy have to be found, namely the transfer of an interest in the estate payment of rent, and the right to possession as against the tenant in respect of the Premises sublet. In assignment the tenant has to divest himself of all the rights that he has as a tenant.

IK-190902:L111.text: The expression "parted with possession" undoubtedly postulates parting with possession session means giving possession to persons other than those to whom possession has been given by lease and "parting with possession" must have been by the tenant.

IK-190902:L112.text: The mere user by other persons is no parting with Possession so long as the tenant retains the legal possession himself or in other words there must be vesting of possession by the tenant in another person by divesting himself not only of physical possession but also of the right to possession. The divestment or abandonment of the right to possession is necessary in order to invoke the clause of parting with possession: See cite11†Hazari Lal v. Gian Ram . 1972 Ren Cr 74 (Delhi).
